input: Pervaporation is a membrane separation process in which a liquid feed is placed in contact with one side of a membrane, while a vacuum applied on the other side draws the permeating component through the membrane as a vapour. In this context, flux refers to the mass permeating per unit membrane area per hour (kg m⁻² h⁻¹), and the separation factor is defined as the water-to-alcohol ratio in the permeate divided by the same ratio in the feed, and is therefore dimensionless. In the work described here, two membranes were compared using a feed of 85 wt% isopropanol in water at 60 °C. The polymer membrane achieved a flux of 2 kg m⁻² h⁻¹ with a separation factor of 180, although its flux fell by 6% over 500 h. The zeolite membrane, by contrast, achieved a flux of 1.1 kg m⁻² h⁻¹ with a separation factor of 560, and its flux remained unchanged over 500 h within measurement error. It is worth noting that only one feed composition was tested, and no test ran beyond 500 h. The figures for the two membranes were obtained on the same feed, and the stability figures cover the same test duration for each membrane, so the comparison between them is a direct one. Overall, flux, selectivity and stability are seldom reported together for the same membrane, which makes comparisons of this kind less complete than they might otherwise be.
target:
Pervaporation separates a liquid mixture through a membrane: the liquid feed contacts one side of the membrane, and vacuum on the other side draws the permeating component through as vapour. Flux denotes the mass permeating per unit membrane area per hour (kg m⁻² h⁻¹), and the separation factor denotes the water-to-alcohol ratio in the permeate divided by the same ratio in the feed. A polymer membrane and a zeolite membrane were compared on a feed of 85 wt% isopropanol in water at 60 °C, both run under the same arrangement, so the comparison is between the membrane materials and not between test conditions.

The polymer membrane gave a flux of 2 kg m⁻² h⁻¹ and a separation factor of 180, and its flux fell 6% over 500 h. The zeolite membrane gave a flux of 1.1 kg m⁻² h⁻¹ and a separation factor of 560, and its flux was unchanged over 500 h within measurement error. The zeolite membrane is the more selective and the more stable of the two; the polymer membrane passes more mass per unit area. The ranking by flux and the ranking by separation factor run in opposite directions, and a selection between the membranes turns on which quantity the separation duty values.

Each membrane's figures were obtained on that feed, and the stability figures cover the same test duration for both membranes. One feed composition was tested, and no test ran beyond 500 h; flux, selectivity and stability are seldom reported together for the same membrane, and the comparison states all three for these two membranes at the tested composition.
